methodological_rigor.justification: This in vitro study of TQ-ox in AGS gastric cancer cells versus normal HGEpiC cells uses a comprehensive battery of validated assays (ATP cytotoxicity, ROS, GSH, MMP, AO/EB apoptosis staining, comet assay). The study uses at least 4 independent experiments with appropriate statistical testing (one-way ANOVA, Tukey post-hoc, Shapiro-Wilk normality). Limitations include exclusive in vitro design without in vivo validation, use of only one cancer cell line (AGS), and modest IC50 differential between cancer and normal cells (40.29 vs 46.42 µM) suggesting limited selectivity.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a preclinical in vitro study, mapping to Oxford LoE 5. The compound TQ-ox shows cytotoxic effects in gastric cancer cells, but the narrow therapeutic window (IC50 40 vs 46 µM) and absence of in vivo pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic data severely limit translational relevance. Gastric cancer is an important clinical target but cell line studies represent early-stage mechanistic work without demonstrated clinical path.

reporting_quality.justification: As a cell-line/in vitro study, ARRIVE guidelines for animal studies are not applicable, but reporting of cell culture conditions, reagent catalog numbers, equipment specifications, and statistical methods is thorough and reproducible. Ethics statement for cell line use is included. Data are not deposited in a public repository and no data availability statement is provided. The synthesis reference for TQ-ox is cited from prior work, with appropriate acknowledgment.

novelty_literature.justification: The extension of TQ-ox characterization to AGS gastric cancer cells represents a meaningful addition to an ongoing series of studies by the same group on TQ-ox across cancer types (melanoma, HepG2, SKOV-3, A549). However, the mechanistic framework (ROS-mediated oxidative stress, GSH depletion, MMP collapse, apoptosis) is highly consistent with prior TQ-ox publications, limiting the novel mechanistic insights. The contribution lies primarily in establishing gastric cancer as an additional susceptible target.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written with well-organized sections. Methods are described with sufficient detail for replication. Results are presented with appropriate statistical notation and dose-response context. The discussion effectively positions findings within the broader TQ-ox literature while acknowledging limitations (in vitro only, single cell line). Figures are referenced in context, though not reproduced here. Minor grammatical issues are present but do not impede comprehension.

key_strengths: Comprehensive multi-endpoint characterization of TQ-ox effects including cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, apoptosis, and genotoxicity in parallel
Inclusion of normal HGEpiC comparison cells with 4+ independent experimental replicates enhances reproducibility
Clear mechanistic framing linking ROS-mediated damage to apoptosis induction
key_concerns: Narrow therapeutic window (IC50 40.29 vs 46.42 µM cancer vs normal cells) raises questions about selectivity for clinical development
Exclusive in vitro design with a single cancer cell line limits generalizability and translational conclusions
Mechanistic findings largely replicate prior TQ-ox publications by the same group with limited new mechanistic insight
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competent incremental in vitro study documenting TQ-ox activity in gastric cancer cells, appropriate for a Tier 3 oncology or pharmacology journal. The comprehensive assay battery and dual cell-line approach support acceptance with minor revisions to better articulate selectivity limitations.
